title: Thermodynamic statistics of given names in USA and France
authors: Klaus M. Frahm, Dima L. Shepelyansky
abstract: Using official government data sets of USA and France we analyze the occurrence/frequency/popularity distributions of given names on a time scale of more than 100 years. These distributions are characterized through the Lorenz and Pareto curves broadly used in the analysis of wealth inequality in the world. These curves remain stable during the considered time period with the Gini coefficient remaining in the narrow range 0.85-0.95. As for the case of wealth inequality, we show that the distributions of names are well described by the Rayleigh-Jeans (RJ) thermalization and condensation phenomenon well studied in various physical systems. The RJ thermalization results from two integrals of motion being analogous to energy and probability norm conservation in physical systems with energy states corresponding to popularity levels of names. Time correlations between names are also determined showing their stability until the middle of the twentieth century and a significant change after that.
summary: This paper treats the popularity distribution of given names in the USA and France as a physical system analogous to wealth inequality. By applying tools from statistical mechanics—specifically Rayleigh-Jeans thermalization theory—the authors demonstrate that name frequencies exhibit remarkable long-term stability. This suggests that naming preferences follow universal, quantifiable thermodynamic laws.
main_problem: The study analyzes the long-term statistical distributions of given names in the USA and France, treating name popularity as an analogue to wealth distribution.
main_result: The name frequency distributions exhibit remarkable stability over more than a century, suggesting they are governed by universal physical principles like Rayleigh-Jeans (RJ) thermalization and condensation.
method: The authors apply concepts from statistical mechanics used in analyzing wealth inequality, such as the Lorenz curve, Gini coefficient, and Pareto distribution, to historical name data.
model_or_system: The system is an analogy: given name frequency ($f_m$) is mapped onto wealth ($w_m$), and the underlying dynamics are modeled using concepts derived from energy conservation in physical systems (RJ thermalization).
key_observables: Lorenz curves, Gini coefficient (stable range of 0.85-0.95), Pareto distribution parameters, and Pearson correlator coefficients ($ho$).
important_parameters: Time scale exceeding 100 years; the RJ model parameters ($T, \mu$ or $a, \epsilon$).
main_assumptions: The core assumption is that name frequency distributions can be accurately modeled using thermodynamic analogies derived from wealth inequality analysis.
figures_summary: Figures show Lorenz and Pareto curves for US/FR names across various years, demonstrating high Gini coefficients and stability. Correlator plots (Fig. 9) track year-to-year correlations.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the analogy between name frequency and wealth distribution, applies statistical tools (Lorenz/Gini), models the dynamics using RJ thermalization theory, and validates this model by fitting parameters to historical data from both countries.
why_interesting: Although applied to sociology, the reliance on established concepts like RJ condensation and entropy conservation provides a novel, non-standard application of statistical physics principles to complex empirical time series.
